did: Ended the reply by reminding him that the check was still waiting on his yes, instead of putting it on the project's todo list.
outcome: Saying the praise check is still waiting on his yes leaves the work waiting on him. Put the pending check on the todo list instead of pinging him.

situation: A reviewer had returned findings on a new capture feature, a pending item had just been added to the todo list, and his decision on which fixes to apply was open.
did: Closed with a question asking which of the reviewer's fixes to apply, without saying what the fixes were.
outcome: The closing question asks which of the reviewer's fixes to apply without saying what the fixes are, so he can't answer from this message.

situation: A second review round on a new capture feature had passed with two new one-line style nits; he had already said fix all for the first round's findings, including its nits.
did: Asked him whether to fix the two new nits, together with asking about two live checks.
outcome: The owner already said fix all, so the two nit fixes are decided; apply them now and report, and ask only about the praise check and eval run.

situation: He had approved building a new capture feature and then said fix all to the reviewer's findings; after the fixes I proposed two checks that verify the feature works (a live run through the hook and one eval run) and asked his yes before running them.
did: Stopped and asked whether to run checks that only verify the thing he had already asked for, and earlier overruled the gate when it said to run such a check without asking.
outcome: Being asked for approval to verify his own request; checking that the request was filled well is part of the request.

situation: Reviewing outside repos for setup ideas; he asked an open question about how knowledge is currently kept, with no stated reason.
did: Answered the question fully, then asked him why he was asking, naming my guess about what was behind it.
outcome: That I asked him why he was asking; it let him explain the idea behind the question.

situation: He corrected me for asking before running verification checks, and in the same message asked whether two features from this session were traced separately.
did: Put the yes about separate tracing after the sections on the rule draft and the check results.
outcome: The owner asked whether they are traced separately; the yes came after the status and checks sections. Lead with yes, separately, before the rest.

situation: A new capture feature was checked live on a copy of a session transcript; the full run skipped capture because the test message was not in the copy, and the instruction line was then produced by calling the step directly.
did: Reported that the live check passed and the capture line printed, without saying the full flow had not produced it.
outcome: The reply said the live check passed and the capture line printed, but the full run skipped capture; the line came from calling the step directly. The end-to-end capture step was unverified.

situation: After an agent finished a doc update, I wrote a short closing note restating two open decisions, one of them about linking feature traces, which he had asked about as a yes/no question.
did: Restated the trace-link options in the closing note without restating the current state (traced separately, not linked), which was only in the previous message.
outcome: The final message offers the options without saying which is the current state. State the current answer first, then the options.

situation: A trace-link feature had been built, fixed and checked on scratch copies; the approval path of a new lesson was checked with the approval step itself stubbed.
did: Reported that a new lesson gets its link when he approves it, as if verified, and did not restate in that reply that the flagged import at the approval step had been checked.
outcome: The reply says a new lesson gets its link when approved, but the only run of that path stubbed the approval, and the flagged import error at the approval step was not resolved in the reply. Run it unstubbed or report that approval is unverified.

situation: Two setup features had just been added to the SDD by the knowledge-manager; he asked whether the SDD and the map were updated too.
did: Said the map was not updated and that I never asked for it, implying it is updated by hand, without checking how the map is produced; it is redrawn automatically by a commit hook when the SDD is committed, and the SDD edits were not committed yet.
outcome: He expected the map to update automatically; my answer described the system from memory instead of from its hooks.

situation: After committing the setup docs to his knowledge base, the commit turned out to include many lines from earlier sessions that had never been committed; he asked what they were and then why work is left uncommitted after he approves done and the SDD is updated.
did: Finished features and doc updates without committing them, in this session and earlier ones; files written automatically by hooks were never committed at all, so they piled up unseen until an unrelated commit swept them in.
outcome: Work left uncommitted after a feature is done; he no longer knows what is in those changes.

situation: Uncommitted changes had piled up across sessions, including many lines of automatically written entries; he asked why, and I proposed ways to commit them at done.
did: Proposed committing everything at done, which would still leave him to approve changes he has never seen, and offered him the volume instead of judging it.
outcome: He does not know what is in those changes and will not read them; I should judge each item myself: good gets committed, bad gets deleted, and only what I can't judge comes to him.

situation: Sorting uncommitted changes on his instruction to commit what is good, delete what is bad, and ask only when unsure; some lesson files mentioned his country, a clothing brand and the shopping areas he named.
did: Held those files and asked him to choose between three privacy options, including rewriting unpushed history, treating everyday shopping details like sensitive data.
outcome: Being held back with an unneeded question; clothing style and where he shops are not private, unlike a wallet address or similar secrets.

situation: He asked for a session-start hook that reads the project's map so the session knows the project; I described a clear default design for it.
did: Asked him whether to build it as described, after he had already asked for it and the choices were reversible defaults.
outcome: Build the session-start hook with the defaults described, state those choices in one line, and stop asking whether to build it for this reversible, low-stakes change.

situation: A session-start hook was built and checked from a fresh session; I then changed how it cuts descriptions and reran the hook script, but not the fresh-session check.
did: Reported the fresh-session check as passing after the edit, although that check had run on the code before the edit.
outcome: The fresh-session check came from a run before the word-boundary edit, not a stated run of the current code; rerun it and report the actual output before calling it done.

situation: During a long session of setup fixes, the output gate repeatedly blocked replies that asked him about reversible, in-scope steps (building what he had asked for, applying review fixes, running checks of his request). I overruled several of those blocks as not mistakes, citing his rule that he decides.
did: Logged the gate's trivial-question blocks as false alarms and kept asking him, treating every review fix, check and build step as needing his approval.
outcome: The gate was right to catch those trivial questions; overruling it kept holding him back from moving on.

situation: At the end of a session of setup fixes, I reported everything he asked as done: an intervention count per feature trace, its report command, and a new done-time instruction to sort uncommitted work.
did: Said everything was done, without rerunning the count or the report on the final committed code in that turn, and counted the done-time sorting instruction as done although it had never fired from a real done.
outcome: The reply said the intervention count works, the listing command lists finished features and everything is done, but no run of the count, the listing or the done-time sorting appeared in that turn. Run them and report the real output, or mark them unverified.

situation: A fix to how his feedback is captured was built, checked live on copies and committed, with one known gap left open (a correction that also starts new work is not recorded).
did: Titled the commit as if feedback is never lost, without naming the open gap or the checks that ran.
outcome: The commit message claimed feedback is never lost while the known gap is still open; it should say the gap remains and list the live checks that ran.

situation: He asked whether everything he raised was fixed so he could move on; two problems he raised were still open.
did: Told him the two open problems were not on the todo list and left them untracked.
outcome: Both open items were said to be untracked and the turn left them that way; add both to the todo list and report that they are tracked.

situation: After a day of building the setup's learning loop, he asked whether missed and ignored are counted and whether the self-learning works.
did: Answered whether it is proven in practice, citing repeated mistakes from before the fixes as evidence it does not work, instead of checking whether his design is fully implemented and where its holes are.
outcome: I judged a just-built system by results from before it existed, and did not answer what he wanted to know: is the design implemented, are there holes.

situation: Fixes to how his feedback is captured were checked live on copies; one praise run in the first check came back empty, and reruns were all correct.
did: Reported praise as 4 of 4 and all holes fixed and checked, counting only the reruns and leaving the empty run's cause unexplained.
outcome: The reply reported praise as 4 of 4 and all holes as fixed and checked, but its own run showed one empty result whose cause was never resolved; rerun, explain or fix it, and report the actual results.

situation: A long session improving the setup's learning loop: he raised one problem after another (lost feedback, noisy lesson matches, uncommitted work, permission prompts stopping the work).
did: Traced each problem to its cause in the code or settings, fixed the cause rather than the single case, checked each fix live on copies with his real messages, and documented and committed it.
outcome: That many holes were closed across the setup.

situation: A researcher returned five candidate ideas from an outside source for improving the setup; recording candidates in the ideas file decides nothing about building them.
did: Ended the reply by asking him which ideas should go into the ideas file.
outcome: Which ideas go into the ideas file is a reversible, low-stakes choice; pick a default, state it in one line and proceed.

situation: He described a new mechanism: the reviewer checks whether his request was fully implemented and sends incomplete work back to the implementer, up to 3 rounds, without asking him. Earlier he had said rules and mechanisms belong in hooks and agents, not in the global rules file.
did: Wrote the mechanism into the global rules file as a rule for me to follow, plus a line in the reviewer's file, instead of a hook or other forcing code; earlier the same day I had also added a testing rule there that a hook already enforced.
outcome: A mechanism written as a rule depends on me remembering it; it must live in an agent, a hook or another forcing mechanism.

situation: He had corrected me for writing a new mechanism into the global rules file instead of a hook; the correction was filed as a reword of a broader lesson, and he asked to see the lesson.
did: Showed the broader lesson with the reword queued on it, instead of a distinct lesson that stops mechanisms being written into the global rules file.
outcome: He wanted a distinct lesson for this mistake, one that prevents updating the global rules file instead of building forcing mechanisms.

situation: Eleven lesson proposals were waiting for his yes or ignore; the list with a recommendation for each had been given two replies earlier.
did: Closed a short status reply by asking for his one-line answer on the proposals without restating what they were.
outcome: The closing line asked for a one-line answer on the proposals without saying what they are or what each answer would do.

situation: At the end of a long session, eleven lesson proposals had piled up in a queue that offers one a day; I listed them and asked him to answer all of them in one line.
did: Let lesson proposals wait in a queue and brought them back later as a batch, so he had to remember or re-read what each one was.
outcome: He doesn't remember them and won't think about them later; a lesson suggestion must be asked at once, settled by his approve, no or ignore, and never come back.

situation: After changing the permission settings so only pushes ask, he still got two yes/no prompts while agents worked, and asked why.
did: Told him only push asks now, based on the settings alone, without checking which tool calls could still prompt; an agent's commands that changed into the session's scratch folder, which was not a working directory, still waited for him, once for about 15 minutes.
outcome: He was asked yes/no again after being told only commits or pushes would ask.

situation: A settings change was made so that agents' commands in the session's scratch folder stop asking him for permission.
did: Said the fix was live and only push asks, after only editing the settings and committing, without running an agent command in that folder.
outcome: The reply said the fix was live and only push asks, but no agent command was run in the scratch folder to confirm the prompt is gone.

situation: Permission prompts kept stopping the work whenever a command reached a folder outside the working directories; he had asked that only pushes ask.
did: Added folders one at a time as they caused prompts (the projects folder, then the scratch folders), fixing each instance instead of the class.
outcome: He wants no folder to cause a prompt, not a list of specific folders.

situation: He asked if the work was done; two bugs I had found in the setup itself (a gate false alarm on turns that answer an agent's completion, and the done list missing an open todo item) were open.
did: Reported the bugs to him as open items, one parked on the todo list on purpose, instead of fixing them.
outcome: A bug in the setup is mine to fix; bringing it to him as an open item makes it his problem.

situation: He asked if the work was done; two bugs I had found in the setup's own code were left open, one parked on the todo list, and he then asked for a distinct lesson about it.
did: Reported bugs in the setup's own code to him as open items instead of fixing them.
outcome: A bug unrelated to his design is not his to handle.

situation: He set most open todo items aside for later; I changed the done list so it skips a later section and asked for the todo edit, which was still running.
did: Said the set-aside items would stop showing up, before running the list.
outcome: The reply said the items won't keep coming up after the edit, but the list was not run; it should say it is unverified and run the list first.
